Comparative Performance Analysis of OpenMP vs. MPI for Data Processing

Author: Vinay V Hiremath (USN: 01FE24BCI069) | Department of Computer Science & Engineering [AI]

Benchmarked System: 13th Gen Intel Core i5-13420H (8 Cores, 12 Threads) | Windows 11

Executive Summary

This report presents an empirical performance evaluation comparing OpenMP (Shared Memory) and MPI (Distributed Memory) paradigms for large-scale data processing workloads. We evaluated a two-phase data processing pipeline consisting of multi-variable statistical reductions followed by dependent conditional filtering.

Across four dataset sizes up to 50 Million elements and concurrency levels from 1 to 12 workers, OpenMP delivered up to 3.27x speedup (25.10 ms) and MPI achieved up to 3.42x speedup (24.00 ms), representing a processing throughput exceeding 2.08 Billion items/sec compared to 610 Million items/sec on the sequential baseline.

1. Problem Definition & Architectural Design

The processing pipeline executes two computational passes over an array of N double-precision floating-point numbers:

  • Pass 1 (Reductions): Accumulates Sum, Sum of Squares, Minimum, and Maximum. Mean, Variance, and Standard Deviation are calculated in O(1) time.
  • Pass 2 (Dependent Filter): Counts elements strictly greater than the dataset mean (x_i > μ).
Dimension OpenMP (Shared Memory) MPI (Distributed Memory)
Memory Model Single shared virtual address space Isolated private address spaces per process
Inter-Worker Communication Implicit via shared RAM/cache reads Explicit message passing (MPI_Reduce, MPI_Bcast)
Data Partitioning Automated loop scheduling (schedule(static)) Manual 1D domain decomposition per rank
Synchronization Implicit pragma barrier at loop termination Explicit collective barriers and reductions

2. Implementation Details

All implementations were engineered in ANSI C, compiled with GCC -O3 optimizations, and verified to yield bitwise identical outputs.

OpenMP Implementation Structure

// Pass 1: Multi-variable parallel reduction
#pragma omp parallel for reduction(+:sum, sum_sq) reduction(min:min_val) reduction(max:max_val) schedule(static)
for (long long i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    double v = data[i];
    sum += v;
    sum_sq += v * v;
    if (v < min_val) min_val = v;
    if (v > max_val) max_val = v;
}

// Pass 2: Filter elements above mean using reduction
#pragma omp parallel for reduction(+:count_above_mean) schedule(static)
for (long long i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    if (data[i] > mean) count_above_mean++;
}

MPI Implementation Structure

// 1D Domain Decomposition
long long base_chunk = N / num_procs;
long long remainder = N % num_procs;
long long local_count = base_chunk + (rank < remainder ? 1 : 0);
long long local_start = rank * base_chunk + (rank < remainder ? rank : remainder);

// Pass 1: Local reductions and collective tree aggregation
MPI_Reduce(&local_sum, &global_sum, 1, MPI_DOUBLE, MPI_SUM, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD);
MPI_Reduce(&local_min, &global_min, 1, MPI_DOUBLE, MPI_MIN, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD);
MPI_Reduce(&local_max, &global_max, 1, MPI_DOUBLE, MPI_MAX, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD);

// Broadcast mean to all ranks for Pass 2 dependency
if (rank == 0) global_mean = global_sum / (double)N;
MPI_Bcast(&global_mean, 1, MPI_DOUBLE, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD);

// Pass 2: Local conditional filter and final reduction
MPI_Reduce(&local_above_count, &global_above_count, 1, MPI_LONG_LONG, MPI_SUM, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD);

Performance Insights

  1. Amdahl's Law Saturation: Speedup scales cleanly up to 4 cores, peaking around 8 cores. Beyond 8 cores, memory bus contention bounds further scaling.
  2. Cache Locality & Isolation: MPI performs well at 50M elements because 1D domain decomposition ensures each process works within its isolated L2/L3 cache footprint.
  3. Efficiency Balance: Parallel efficiency remains above 75% at 4 cores, identifying 4-8 workers as the optimal operational point.
